newsitem.title: USA: Big Oil's efforts fail to boost black employment.
newsitem.headline: Big Oil's efforts fail to boost black employment.

text.p: Efforts by major U.S. oil companies to help programs targeting minority students for high-skilled industry jobs have failed to boost the number of blacks graduating with engineering degrees.

The major companies have a prominent role on the boards and donor lists of many minority education groups, including Texaco Inc., which was singled out by the head of the National Action Council for Minorities in Engineering (NACME) as an "amazing supporter" donating over $1 million in 20 years.
However, the ranks of blacks leaving school with degrees for oil jobs has remained in single digits for years.

In 1995, nine blacks graduated in petroleum engineering throughout the entire country and in 1993 only three, according to Charles Walker, executive director of the National Society of Black Engineers in Alexandria, Va.
Nationally, 281 students graduated with petroleum engineering degrees in 1995, with 22 of that number minorities, which includes blacks, American Indians and Hispanics, a researcher for NACME said.
"Big Oil" was thrust into the racial spotlight when Texaco Inc. executives were allegedly taped mocking blacks and destroying documents to derail an anti-discrimination lawsuit filed by employees.
Civil rights leader Jesse Jackson and others called for a national boycott of Texaco service stations and products until the issues were settled.

Then, on Nov. 15. Texaco reached the biggest settlement of a racial discrimination case in the United States, agreeing to pay $176 million to settle the lawsuit, which charged it had systematically discriminated against blacks and denied them promotions.

At the recently held annual gathering of the American Petroleum Institute in Washington, Exxon Corp. Chairman Lee Raymond blamed a faulty education system for the lack of minorities in what he called a largely technical business.

Minority education leaders said Raymond's comments partially explain the problem, but leave out the key historical and cultural blocks that work against blacks in the oil industry and in the broader engineering field.

"There are not many role-models for African-Americans in engineering. For African-Americans looking for a hard field, there has not been much attention to engineering, not much accolade and honor," Walker said.
He said that has changed somewhat in the last 10 years. As technology has risen to the forefront, so has recognition of engineering as an education choice.
"This will be the first generation of African-Americans looking at engineering as an education," said Walker.
U.S. government statistics show that out of 1.815 million Americans working as engineers in 1994, around 3 percent were blacks.

NACME noted, however, that the number of minority engineering graduates rose to 9 percent of all engineers in 1995, and outright numbers moved from 1,423 in 1974 to an all-time high of 5,931 last year.

"Traditionally, (minorities) are more underepresented in the engineering field, and if you look at people with petroleum engineering degrees, they are even more underepresented," said NACME President George Campbell.
But, Campbell does not point the finger at oil companies, at least not in the last two decades. He said the major oil companies have been supportive.

"From my point of view you can take any large corporation in the United States and find individuals with that point of view (alleged racist comments on the Texaco tapes)," Campbell said, adding "it was unfair to single out the oil industry."

"From the very beginning, the oil industry has been the largest supporter of this effort (NACME), and they have recognized the need to develop more minority talent. It is just in their self-interest," Campbell said.
He noted Exxon Senior Vice President Edwin Hess was on the NACME board of directors and would soon assume the chairmanship.
Campbell said historical exclusion and the lack of science and math schooling for young minority students thwarts the number of minorities entering the engineering industry.
